title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the sources. No licensing agreements with rights holders were in place for that material. The failure is not in the model's output logic but in the input pipeline: copyrighted recordings were used as training data without permission, and the resulting system can reproduce recognizable sections of specific songs when prompted with descriptions of genre, era, and artist style.

This kind of failure is detectable at the design stage, not after deployment. A rights-clearance review of training data sources, conducted before scraping began, would have identified the problem. The fact that record labels were able to recreate close imitations of named works using ordinary prompts suggests the model memorized or closely encoded source material rather than abstracting general musical patterns. A German court ruled against Suno on copyright grounds in a case brought by GEMA, one label group settled with Suno and formed a joint venture, and another settled with Udio, while additional lawsuits from independent artists and music publishers remain active.

What is not established is whether any court outside Germany has issued a final verdict finding copyright infringement, whether the fair-use defense will ultimately succeed or fail in U.S. proceedings, or what the full terms of the settlements are.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, alleging the companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their systems. The labels claim both companies deliberately concealed their training data and that the services directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The lawsuits reference massive catalogs including works by The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey, among many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like genre, era, and artist style. Examples include generating songs that closely mimicked Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and Green Day's "American Idiot," sometimes reproducing entire lyrics and melodies. The companies have been sued in New York and Massachusetts, and the labels submitted a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence. Both Udio and Suno previously claimed their training practices constitute fair use.
